title: Read the notes, not the waveform
allegory: A Fourier basis is like describing a sound by the notes being played instead of the air pressure at every instant: the waveform is a dense, busy wiggle, but written as sheet music it is a handful of notes, and that short list is what you can actually read.
map: the air pressure at each of 113 instants
the standard basis: one row per input number 0 to 112
the pure notes you are allowed to use
the Fourier basis: a constant, plus cos and sin at each frequency k = 1 to 56
rewriting the recording as how loud each note is
multiplying by the basis matrix: W_E in Fourier coordinates
only the key frequencies (14, 31, 35, 41, 42, 52) have non-trivial norm
the notes all peaking together on one beat
constructive interference: the key waves line up only at z = x + y mod 113

cap.1: A tiny model has learned to add on a 113-hour clock. Its weights look like static: every entry busy, no pattern anywhere. How do you read that?
cap.2: Nanda et al.'s one-layer transformer learned x + y mod 113. Laid out one row per input number, its embedding matrix looks dense and patternless.
cap.3: Inputs [x, y, =], vocabulary 114, and all 12,769 input pairs fit in one batch. In the token basis W_E is dense; the structure appears only after a change of basis.

cap.1: A recording looks like a busy wiggle. Written as sheet music it is a handful of notes. Same sound, different description, and one is far easier to read.
cap.2: A change of basis: describe each input number not by its position, but by how much of each wave, a cos and a sin at each frequency, it contains.
cap.3: Periodic in the standard basis means sparse in the Fourier basis, and sparsity is what makes the weights readable.

cap.1: The notes you may use: one flat line, then a cosine and a sine wave at each speed from 1 to 56. That makes 113 waves for 113 numbers: a full set.
cap.2: Row 0 is the constant; rows 2k−1 and 2k are cos and sin at frequency k. Normalise each row and the 113 × 113 basis is orthonormal, so nothing is lost.
cap.3: Stack the rows into F; W_E in Fourier coordinates is F @ W_E over the 113 number tokens. Outside the exercise, an FFT (torch.fft) gives the same coefficients up to scaling and sign.

chapters.name: Six notes light up
chapters.title: which of the 56 frequencies the embedding keeps

cap.1: Rewrite the embedding in waves and almost everything goes quiet. Of 56 speeds, only 6 carry real weight: 14, 31, 35, 41, 42 and 52.
cap.2: Take the norm of each row of Fourier-space W_E. Only the cos and sin rows of a handful of key frequencies stand out; the model discarded the rest.
cap.3: In ARENA's checkpoint the key frequencies are 14, 31, 35, 41, 42 and 52. Neurons cluster by these frequencies, and W_logit reads only cos(w_k z) and sin(w_k z) for them.

chapters.name: Off by one

left.title: Raw argmax index
lines: every later step at the wrong frequency

chapters.verdict: Check a claimed frequency by projecting onto it: a wrong one projects to almost nothing.

cap.1: Count the notes from the wrong starting key and every answer comes out one too low. Nothing looks broken, which is the danger.
cap.2: The 2D Fourier helper's slice 0 holds frequency k = 1. Argmax over it, use the raw index, and every key frequency is one low. Add one.
cap.3: Otherwise the trig sum directions, restricted loss and excluded loss are all computed at the wrong frequencies. Project the logits onto cos(w_k(x+y)): a wrong k gives near-zero norm.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The right basis turns static into a short list
Read the mechanism, then measure it

cap.1: The trick outlives this toy: when weights look like static, try describing them in another vocabulary. The right one can make a mess sparse.
cap.2: With the Fourier view, Nanda et al. read off the whole algorithm, then built progress measures that move long before test loss does.
cap.3: For understanding and steering AI: much of interpretability is finding the basis where a computation is sparse, from Fourier modes here to sparse autoencoder features.

coda.title: Logits as waves: the answer is where the key-frequency waves line up

curves.label: sum of the first m key waves

readouts.label: best score for any wrong answer

caption.1: Across is how far a guess is from the true answer. One wave peaks at the answer but nearly as high elsewhere. Add waves and only the answer stays tall.
caption.2: The grokked model scores each possible answer z by summing cos(w(x + y − z)) over its key frequencies. The waves all agree only at z = x + y mod 113.
caption.3: At offset 0 every cosine is 1, so the score is m; elsewhere the phases scatter and partly cancel. With one frequency the best wrong answer nearly ties (margin 0.002).

where_else: Audio and image compression, which store a few strong frequencies instead of every sample
Sparse autoencoders: learning a basis in which a model's activations become sparse and readable
Progress measures for grokking: metrics built from the Fourier circuit that move long before test loss does

hamming.what: Re-expressing a matrix indexed by input number in terms of waves, a constant plus a cosine and sine at each frequency, so periodic structure shows up as a few large entries.
hamming.when: When inputs live on a circle, as in modular arithmetic, or when weights look like dense static that may be periodic underneath.
hamming.why: A good basis turns a dense, unreadable matrix into a short list, and that list is what let Nanda et al. read the grokked model's whole algorithm.

object.title: The tuning comb
object.subtitle: A toy embedding with 11 inputs and 8 model directions: turn the knob to redescribe the same weights row by row in waves (label: input / wave).
object.f: (1 - t) * abs(Math.cos(4 * PI * r / 11 - c) + 0.6 * Math.cos(10 * PI * r / 11 - 2 * c)) + t * 2.345 * (r == 3 ? abs(Math.cos(c)) : r == 4 ? abs(Math.sin(c)) : r == 9 ? 0.6 * abs(Math.cos(2 * c)) : r == 10 ? 0.6 * abs(Math.sin(2 * c)) : 0)

knobs.label: description: 0 = a row per input, 1 = a row per wave

cap.1: A toy embedding: one row per input number 0 to 10, one column per model direction. Every bar is busy; nothing stands out.
cap.2: p = 11 instead of 113, so it fits on a table. Bar height is the size of each weight. In the standard basis it looks dense.
cap.3: The periodic structure is smeared across every token row, so no single entry is informative on its own.

cap.1: Describe each column in waves instead: only four rows stand up, a cos and a sin at two frequencies. Everything else is flat.
cap.2: The same matrix after F @ W_E. Only this toy's key frequencies, 2 and 5, carry weight.
cap.3: An orthonormal change of basis keeps the total squared weight (Parseval) but concentrates it in a few rows, so the bars get taller.

cap.1: Halfway between the two descriptions, the busy bars drain into a few rows.
cap.2: The knob only blends the two pictures to show where the weight goes; the real change of basis is one matrix multiply.
cap.3: F is orthogonal and acts along the token axis, so the change of basis loses nothing and Fᵀ undoes it.

cap.1: From above: two pairs of rows, like two notes, each a cos and a sin. The pair lets a wave start at any point in its cycle.
cap.2: A cos and a sin at the same frequency together make a wave with any phase shift, which is why key frequencies come in pairs of rows.
cap.3: a·cos(wx) + b·sin(wx) = R·cos(wx − φ): the pair (a, b) is an amplitude and a phase, so frequency k uses rows 2k−1 and 2k.

cap.1: In the real model there are 113 rows and six key frequencies: 14, 31, 35, 41, 42 and 52.
cap.2: Nanda et al.'s grokked model keeps only those; its neurons and its unembedding use the same frequencies.
cap.3: W_logit times the Fourier basis transpose is zero except at columns 2k−1 and 2k for the key frequencies k.

predict.q: You change basis from input numbers to waves. How much information is lost?

options.t: None: the basis is orthonormal, so the change can be undone
Some: only the main waves are kept

predict.why: A constant plus cos and sin for k = 1 to 56 gives 113 orthonormal vectors that span everything. The sparsity comes from the model, not the transform.

predict.q: Your key frequencies come out as 13, 30, 34, 40, 41 and 51. What happened?

options.t: An off-by-one: the helper's slice 0 holds frequency 1

predict.why: Add one to the argmaxed indices, then confirm by projecting the logits onto cos(w_k(x+y)): a wrong k gives near-zero norm.

predict.q: Why do key frequencies show up as pairs of rows?

options.t: A cos and a sin together can make a wave at any phase
Each frequency is stored twice for safety

predict.why: a·cos(wx) + b·sin(wx) is one wave with an amplitude and a phase shift, so each frequency needs both rows.
